report:
## Conclusion

The claim that eating dark chocolate lowers the risk of stroke is **moderately supported by observational evidence but not yet confirmed by large randomized trials**.

Multiple observational studies and meta-analyses have found an inverse association between chocolate consumption and stroke risk. A meta-analysis of five prospective studies found a relative risk of 0.81 for high versus low chocolate consumption, and 0.86 for every additional 50 g/week of chocolate intake (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1696220/full). Another analysis found that those eating the highest amount of chocolate had a 17% lower risk of stroke compared to non-consumers (https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/1099). Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses support this inverse association between chocolate intake and cardiovascular events, including stroke (https://www.bmj.com/content/343/bmj.d4488; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8470865/).

The proposed mechanism involves cocoa flavanols, which may lower blood pressure, improve endothelial function, and reduce blood clot formation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11992872/; https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/aug/29/chocolate-reduces-risk-of-strokes-for-men).

However, important caveats remain. Large randomized trials, including the COSMOS trial, have yielded modest, nonsignificant results for cardiovascular event prevention (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10654-026-01382-6). Most evidence comes from observational studies, which cannot establish causation, and many studies examine chocolate generally rather than dark chocolate specifically. Results across studies remain inconsistent (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/9/7/688).

**Bottom line**: Dark chocolate consumption is associated with lower stroke risk in observational research, but definitive causal evidence from large randomized trials is lacking. Moderate consumption of high-cocoa dark chocolate may offer cardiovascular benefits, but it should not be relied upon as a primary stroke prevention strategy.
